text: The only hormone that will make you gain weight and increase your size, in my view, is insulin. No other hormone does that.
It is insulin that increases your body size and makes you look swollen.
It builds fat and glycogen; it is a storage hormone.
They found, by accident, that when antibiotics are given...
chickens and chicks grow faster. People explained it through the microbiota and changes in bacteria.
They say the antibiotic kills harmful bacteria and beneficial bacteria become more active. I don't think that is the whole story.
An antibiotic enters the body and creates an imbalance in the bacterial flora.
Bacteria and fungi normally exist in interacting communities and support one another.
That contributes to digestion and intestinal function. If that balance is disturbed, you can get what I call misdigestion...
incomplete digestion and difficulty with absorption. That disturbance creates a kind of traffic jam.
A traffic jam in the intestines makes the body feel as if food is constantly backed up.
So, in my explanation, insulin keeps being stimulated and weight increases.
Insulin should switch on with eating and off with fasting.
But if the microbiota is disturbed and you develop misdigestion and malabsorption, you create a blockage.
Whether that blockage is in the small intestine or colon, I believe it sends a signal to endocrine cells.
The signal is that food is still present, so a storage hormone is needed.
And the storage hormone is insulin. This is why some people say they eat only once a day...
yet still gain weight. Someone may say, 'I only eat salad and yogurt at night; almost no calories.'
Or, 'I do intermittent fasting and eat only a quarter chicken, yet I still gain weight.'
My explanation is that certain foods keep the intestines obstructed, so the body keeps signaling that food is present and insulin is released.
The same idea applies after antibiotics: bacterial function is disturbed. Remember, digestion does not depend on your body alone.
What does it depend on? First, digestive enzymes.
Second, bacteria and fungi also participate, because your own enzymes do not break down every part of your food.
Take meat fibers: turning a piece of meat into amino acids requires extensive breakdown.
Not all of it is broken down immediately. The stomach churns it and adds acid...
and enzymes to break the meat into smaller components before it moves into the small intestine.
Then additional enzymes come from the pancreas, which releases them through its ducts.
Trypsin enzymes break down proteins. A muscle cell also contains a nucleus and other components.
DNA and RNA need their own enzymes, such as DNases and RNases.
Those enzymes also come from the pancreas. So not everything is necessarily fully digested in the stomach.
There is no guarantee that the stomach alone breaks down all food completely.
If food remains insufficiently digested, problems may occur farther along the intestines. Chewing is therefore important.
Saliva also contains enzymes, so digestion begins with your own enzymes.
And with the microorganisms living with you. If antibiotics suppress those bacteria, you depend more heavily on your own enzymes.
That can lead, in my description, to incomplete digestion and intestinal difficulty.
You can feel intestinal discomfort because the intestines are very sensitive to these changes.
That is why antibiotics can sometimes be followed by loose stools or diarrhea.
In that situation, one microbial group may become dominant over another.
One group appears stronger because the competing group was weakened, and then you experience the consequences.
After long-term antibiotic treatment, for example after prolonged penicillin use...
doctors may prescribe an antifungal such as Diflucan because of fungal overgrowth.
That reflects an alteration in the balance among these microbial communities, and in animals it can also affect weight.
I once mentioned an American man I met not long ago.
He earns substantial money from his business, and he did not want to put all of it directly into the bank.
So he would buy some cattle, keep them for a few weeks or a month, and then sell them.
He would collect them on a farm, feed them for a short period, then resell them.
During those few weeks, he was not set up with proper pasture or grass.
So what did he do? He bought leftover croissants...
pizza and pastries from restaurants and shops, collecting discarded bakery food.
He told me seriously that he obtained these leftovers cheaply or for free and fed them to the livestock.
He said the strange thing was that the animals loved eating them.
And within two weeks, their weight increased significantly.
For him as a trader, those few weeks produced profit and helped cover his costs.
Because it worked financially, he extended the feeding period and even filmed himself doing it.
When he arrived in his Jeep and opened the back, the cattle and sheep would run toward him.
They were waiting for the cake and pizza he had brought.
In my view, he was manipulating the animals' natural feeding patterns in order to increase their size.
He also raised chickens and had a pond nearby with tilapia-like fish.
He would feed the baked leftovers to the animals.
He would feed chickens flour-based feed, and the chickens would produce waste into the pond.
The fish would eat that waste. In a few weeks he could sell chickens, fish, and cattle.
I described it as a distorted ecosystem, and he himself was also overweight.
He was not eating the same feed, of course, but I saw a connection in the overall food system.
In my view, if we feed animals in unhealthy ways and then eat those animals, we participate in the same cycle.
I argued that the resulting meat is no longer the kind of meat people traditionally ate.
My father used to say that meat was no longer like it used to be: the fibers were thicker and the texture had changed.
It also took longer to cook, suggesting to me that the texture itself had changed.
I compared that with how body tissue can also change under different feeding conditions.
If someone can raise a chick into a three-kilogram chicken in thirty days, they can also rapidly fatten other animals.
I make a similar observation about infants fed formula and given antibiotics: some appear unusually puffy or swollen.
The cheeks may become large and red and the arms thick. I do not consider that the natural appearance of a healthy infant.
Later people may say the child has bone problems. I connect this with things that disturb the intestines.
In my view, both antibiotics and formula can contribute to intestinal disturbance and increased body size.
It is the same general idea as the cattle-feeding example I just described.
Another ironic point is that this same man was overweight, so I started talking to him about it.
He said he wanted his body to look leaner like mine. I joked that he could not keep eating badly and expect that.
He asked, 'Then what are we supposed to eat?' I told him I was about to explain it.
I told him not to eat the meat he had produced that way, because I believed it would harm him.
I described that meat as 'poisoned' and said it was no longer performing the nutritional role he expected.
If it is not giving you the benefit you expect, I asked, why eat it?
At duck or swan ponds, and even at wildlife parks, you often see signs saying, 'Please don't feed bread.'
I interpret that as concern about intestinal blockage from bread.
And I argue that this digestive obstruction can have hormonal consequences.
Insulin, in my description, is meant to rise briefly for only a few minutes and then be cleared by the liver.
So it should not remain elevated long enough to continuously create subcutaneous or visceral fat.
But if the insulin system keeps running continuously, fat storage continues.
At the same time, it pulls glucose, amino acids, and other nutrients from the blood.
I describe them as being stored mainly in the liver, fat tissue, and muscles, producing fatty changes.
In my model, this leads to fatty liver and increasing body fat.
That is how I explain areas of fat that seem resistant to loss even during fasting.
You may be fasting, but I argue that your body can still behave as though you have eaten.
I mention bodybuilders who may use insulin before a competition.
If the event is delayed, they may become dizzy and then quickly eat sugary foods afterward.
So a person may look fit while still being harmed metabolically.
In my explanation, persistent insulin elevation suppresses other hormonal systems.
I refer to sex hormones, growth hormone, and thyroid-related hormones as becoming less active.
So I describe continuously high insulin as a stress state for the body.
My goal is to clear the intestines so that fasting is truly recognized and insulin switches off.
Then the other hormonal systems can function. That is why I sometimes advise exercising while fasting.
I might suggest exercising after around six hours without food, with an empty stomach, because I believe the muscles perform better then.
When insulin rises, I say it signals the rest of the body to reduce activity and less blood goes to the muscles.
More blood is concentrated around the intestines as nutrients are being handled and stored in the liver.
So when insulin is down, I describe the rest of the body as more activated.
I say insulin should rise temporarily, mainly with eating, and act first in the liver's circulation.
I argue that giving insulin from outside the body is different from how the body normally produces and uses it.
In my view, excessive insulin treatment can deprive cells of glucose, amino acids, and other basic nutrients.
That can cause confusion, dizziness, blurred vision, and a sense that the body's cells are being starved.
I also say that leg cramps may disappear after following the system and restoring intestinal function.
The bacterial and fungal flora—the microbiota or microbiome—then return to what I consider a healthier balance.
And I describe digestion and absorption as becoming ready to work properly again.
Food is not digested by your own enzymes alone; I describe digestion as happening in several stages, beginning with chewing.
It also involves your enzymes, stomach acids, and the bacteria living with you.
There are trillions of bacteria in the intestines and colon, not a small number.
I mention figures such as around 38 trillion human cells and roughly 45 trillion bacteria.
[Laughter] Look at him today—he looks much better, and even his muscles and body shape have changed.
He says he is not training much, but I tell him the puffiness has gone and he looks more defined.
I say that, God willing, this problem should not return unless he goes back to the things that caused it.
[Laughter] Then the conversation shifts, with a joking reference to shrimp and vaping.
The interviewer says he wants to ask specifically about type 1 diabetes because insulin is central to that discussion.
I reply that we have just discussed insulin, and ask what specific explanation he wants.
He says people have asked him directly and want to hear a fuller explanation from me.
We begin by stepping back from the label and discussing the broader idea of insulin and blood sugar.
I use the example of a tiger eating meat and say that if it is stressed, its blood sugar will rise.
If it is about to attack prey, stress itself can raise glucose. The interviewer asks again about type 1 diabetes.
I say we need to take one step back before discussing 'type 1' because I question that classification itself.
I argue that what is called type 1 is simply an earlier presentation of the same underlying problem.
Medicine divided diabetes into insulin-dependent and non-insulin-dependent forms, then later recognized that many type 2 patients also use insulin.
I say this makes the classification confusing and that the central issue is simply a state of hyperglycemia.
In other words, a state of high blood sugar—that is the condition being discussed.
One person may be started on insulin and another on medication, and then they are labeled type 1 or type 2.
I point out that what is called type 1 can appear at age five, fifteen, or twenty.
Then it may be called late-onset diabetes while still being categorized as type 1, which I question.
They may say insulin was started at age eighteen because the diabetes appeared late.
Then genetics or other explanations are invoked, and today there are several different diabetes categories, including gestational diabetes.
My own concept is simple: when the body needs glucose, it can produce it and raise blood glucose.
For example, before exercise Faisal might have a usual glucose reading around 120.
During exercise, I say it might rise to 200 or 250.
The body needs glucose and can produce it even when the person has not eaten and is fasting.
So I argue that insulin should be very low during fasting, and therefore fasting glucose cannot simply be explained by insulin at that moment.
Insulin will be secreted when food is eaten. I ask: when would I, Diaa, release insulin?
My answer is: when I eat. Then I compare a child labeled diabetic with an adult who is not.
I use the conventional labels only for the sake of discussion.
If both of us have been fasting for six hours, then we compare fasting glucose.
If yours is 300 and mine is 120, the usual explanation is that your insulin is deficient.
But I argue that during fasting insulin is already supposed to be very low, so what exactly are we measuring?
I say the real question should be: why is the glucose high, rather than blaming a hormone that is barely present.
During fasting, I argue that insulin should not be treated as the only explanation.
We measure fasting and post-meal glucose, and fasting and post-meal insulin, but not every other hormone this way.
For example, we do not usually speak of 'fasting testosterone' and 'fed testosterone' in the same way.
I argue that fasting insulin should be close to zero and that each hormone has its own physiological pattern.
Testosterone is different, I say, because it is a systemic hormone circulating more continuously.
It circulates in the main bloodstream, so testosterone can be measured in blood at different times.
I describe insulin instead as closely tied to the gut and feeding state, since we speak of fasting and post-meal insulin.
That is why I call it, in my own terminology, a gut-related hormone.
I argue that if it were presented that way, it would be harder to promote the idea that insulin is universally required to get glucose into cells.
I reject the statement that insulin is always necessary for glucose to enter every cell.
I say that studies are often summarized too broadly when they claim insulin is the hormone responsible for glucose entry into all cells.
I point to red blood cells, brain cells, and other tissues that take up glucose without insulin.
I also mention kidney and intestinal cells as examples of tissues with insulin-independent glucose uptake.
So where does insulin matter for glucose entry? I say especially in certain storage tissues.
I describe the liver as having one route for glucose entry and an additional insulin-sensitive route.
I say the purpose is to capture nutrients after eating before they are lost from the circulation.
After a meal, insulin helps store glucose and amino acids so they can be used later when you are hungry.
I ask whether this explanation is clear before continuing.
Then I compare two people, one fasting with a glucose of 300 and another with a glucose around 100.
By conventional standards, one is normal and the other is diabetic.
I agree the glucose is high, but I ask why it is high rather than stopping at the explanation of 'low insulin.'
I argue that if both people are fasting and insulin is low in both, insulin alone cannot explain the difference.
The interviewer asks whether we are talking about HbA1c; I clarify that at this point I mean ordinary blood glucose.
I then say the situation should be viewed as increased glucose production.
In my model, the issue is increased production rather than simply reduced cellular entry.
If HbA1c is also high, remember that HbA1c is measured in red blood cells.
Blood is tissue, not just water; it contains cellular components and plasma.
The plasma is where the blood glucose reading of 300 is measured, while HbA1c reflects glucose attached to hemoglobin inside red blood cells.
So one value is extracellular and the other is associated with material inside a cell.
If you say HbA1c is high because insulin is low, I ask how glucose got into the red blood cell in the first place.
If insulin were absolutely necessary for glucose entry into every cell, the presence of glucose inside red cells would contradict that simple claim.
I then say that after insulin treatment, plasma glucose may fall from 300 toward 100 and HbA1c may later fall as well.
So, in my argument, the treatment changes both circulating glucose and glucose associated with cells.
I use that to question a simplistic explanation of insulin's role.
I say the patient may feel unwell soon after insulin because of rapid changes in glucose availability.
I describe this as cellular starvation, with brain cells among the first to complain.
Then I return to my broader theory: I describe red blood cells as transporters.
There are trillions of red blood cells; mature red blood cells have no nucleus and have a limited lifespan.
I refer to a lifespan of roughly ninety days in this discussion.
They eventually die, and much of their internal content is the protein hemoglobin.
I describe them as disc-shaped cells moving through the blood and occupying a large proportion of blood volume.
I remind the interviewer that I discussed this transport idea in a previous podcast.
I ask him to imagine a red blood cell carrying glucose.
Now imagine it approaching a brain, kidney, lung, or other body cell.
The red blood cell comes close to that tissue cell.
Between them are plasma, tissue fluid, and the surrounding cellular environment.
Now the two sides need to exchange substances.
I describe the red blood cell as delivering oxygen and glucose.
I say glucose associated with hemoglobin is released toward the plasma and then into the surrounding fluid.
The target cell takes up what it needs; I describe this as a sequence of several transfer steps beginning with the red blood cell.
The two key substances I focus on are glucose and oxygen.
I characterize the red blood cell primarily as a transporter carrying these substances.
I say it carries glucose in association with hemoglobin/HbA1c and also carries oxygen.
Oxygen comes from the lungs, while I describe glucose as coming from the liver.
I imagine delivering those substances to a nerve cell—Faisal—while the red blood cell travels through the plasma.
As it approaches, it releases oxygen and glucose into the plasma and surrounding fluid.
These substances diffuse through the capillary environment and dissolve in the tissue fluid.
The nerve cell then takes them up; that is the first side of the exchange.
After using glucose, the cell produces water and carbon dioxide as end products.
Those waste products move into the surrounding fluid and are picked up by the returning capillary blood.
Red blood cells that have released their cargo then pick up carbon dioxide.
I describe carbon dioxide binding to hemoglobin and water affecting the red blood cell's volume.
The blood then returns through the veins. That is the circulation I am describing.
So the red blood cell delivers glucose and oxygen and then helps carry away waste products.
If this exchange does not proceed properly, I say the tissues become impaired because carbon dioxide and water accumulate.
Those products need to be removed continuously.
Otherwise the process is disrupted. I criticize explanations that discuss oxygen delivery but treat glucose delivery differently.
I argue that glucose is also transported in relation to hemoglobin, not only freely in plasma.
The interviewer says the idea is clear.
I emphasize that point and then move to another claim involving the proportion of glucose produced internally.
While we are talking, neither of us has eaten recently, yet I say much of our circulating glucose is being produced by the liver.
If I am fasting, I ask, where else would the glucose come from throughout the day?
I focus especially on brain and nerve cells because their glucose consumption is very high.
I cite a figure of about five milligrams...
five milligrams of glucose per 100 grams of tissue per minute for brain tissue.
So 100 grams of brain tissue, in this example, uses about five milligrams per minute.
With an average adult brain weighing around 1.5 kilograms, I calculate a substantial daily glucose requirement.
I estimate roughly 125 to 130 grams of glucose per day for the brain alone.
I say dietary sugar is only part of the story because the body also has its own glucose-producing system.
I describe the liver as collecting metabolic substrates such as glycerol, amino acids, and other compounds.
It then continually produces glucose.
I describe that glucose as entering plasma and then associating with red blood cells and hemoglobin.
In my model, hemoglobin carries glucose from the liver and oxygen from the lungs to the body's organs.
And this process is not only for the brain; all body cells require delivery of fuel and oxygen.
I argue that glucose entry into many cells must be hormonally independent, otherwise essential tissues could fail whenever insulin is low.
If the brain required insulin every moment just to receive glucose, then absence of insulin would be immediately catastrophic.
So I say the conventional explanation is incomplete, and I return to the question of HbA1c.
The usual explanation, as I describe it, is that glucose rises first in plasma because it cannot enter cells.
But I ask: if glucose cannot enter cells, how does it enter brain, kidney, and lung cells?
Clearly glucose does enter those tissues, so the simple explanation does not account for everything.
I then try to explain the situation differently.
If glucose simply rose in plasma first and were then pushed into cells, as some people imagine...
why do we sometimes see normal plasma glucose while HbA1c remains elevated?
That suggests, in my interpretation, that the red blood cell is actively taking up and retaining glucose.
I argue that water-soluble substances such as glucose and salts generally cross cell membranes through protein channels or transporters.
They do not simply diffuse freely through the membrane in the same way as gases.
I say only certain substances, especially water and gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide, cross very easily.
They must move rapidly, because failure to exchange oxygen, carbon dioxide, or water would quickly damage cells.
Likewise, if a cell cannot get rid of excess water, it can swell and fail; I use that to illustrate why rapid exchange matters.
So water and dissolved gases can cross membranes readily.
Oxygen and carbon dioxide are the main gases I am referring to.
Other dissolved substances—salts, glucose, potassium, chloride, and similar solutes—are handled through selective permeability.
We learned that the cell membrane has selective permeability.
So if glucose is high inside the red blood cell while plasma glucose is normal, I interpret that as selective uptake by the cell.
I say this can also be seen in situations such as hemorrhage, when the number of red blood cells decreases.
The remaining red blood cells may then carry a greater load.
If there were 100,000 'soldiers' and some were lost through bleeding...
the remaining cells have to carry more of the work that the lost cells would have done.
So, in my analogy, each remaining red blood cell may carry more glucose.
I argue that this differs from the claim that plasma glucose simply rises first and then forces glucose into cells.
If red blood cells are reduced by bleeding or destruction, the remaining cells may carry more, so HbA1c can behave differently from plasma glucose.
I mention pregnancy as another situation in which HbA1c and plasma glucose may not move together in a simple way.
If HbA1c rises while plasma glucose is normal, I take that as evidence that the cell regulates glucose uptake.
The interviewer says he understands the point.
I say it makes more sense to think of the cell as choosing what it takes up rather than having glucose forcibly pushed into it.
Water-soluble substances enter through protein transporters or channels, not by simply being forced through the membrane.
By protein channels, I mean membrane proteins that act like small tubes through the cell membrane.
These transporters open and close in regulated ways.
I say moving glucose into the cell requires energy and controlled transport.
So I reject the idea that glucose is simply forced into cells because its concentration is high outside.
To me, HbA1c is one of the observations that challenges that simplified explanation.
If HbA1c reflects glucose already associated with material inside the red blood cell, then the idea that glucose cannot enter cells is incomplete.
When insulin or glucose-lowering medication reduces blood glucose, I describe it as shifting glucose away from the circulation.
As plasma glucose falls, I argue that red blood cells may release some of the glucose they are carrying.
I compare that with a concentration gradient: when a nearby tissue such as Faisal's needs glucose, glucose moves down the gradient toward it.
I use the term concentration gradient to describe glucose moving from a higher concentration toward a lower one.
In my analogy, insulin diverts glucose from the main circulation into storage in liver, muscle, and fat.
That lowers circulating glucose and changes the gradient.
So, in my model, red blood cells then release more of what they are carrying to restore balance.
I say this is why people taking glucose-lowering medicines may also develop anemia, although that claim requires independent medical evaluation.
I argue that reducing available glucose can stress red blood cells and other tissues.
I then discuss glucose transporters, saying there are multiple transporter proteins for glucose.
I mention that more than a dozen different GLUT transporters have been identified.
Different tissues express different transporters.
I give examples such as GLUT1 in some tissues, GLUT2 in the intestine, GLUT3 in the brain, and others in the kidney.
I then focus on GLUT4 as the transporter that is especially insulin-sensitive.
I say GLUT4 is found mainly in a limited set of tissues, including muscle and fat, and I also discuss the liver in this context.
I compare this to having two doors into a room: a usual route and an extra route that opens in certain conditions.
In muscle, I say glucose can enter through its usual transport mechanisms even without that extra route.
When insulin rises, GLUT4 provides an additional route for glucose uptake.
I argue that GLUT4's special role is mainly important around feeding and storage.
I then restate the point and ask whether Tarek is following the explanation.
[Laughter] I joke about Faisal and say glucose is valuable and appears in two situations in my analogy.
One situation is when the body makes glucose for its own needs, and another is when glucose comes from food.
When glucose comes from food, I say the body wants to store the excess quickly.
I compare glucose to a valuable currency that you do not want to waste.
If someone gave you ten dollars every hour, you would probably save some rather than throw it away.
You would keep it for later when you need it.
In the same way, after eating, the body has extra glucose that it can store.
I compare that to opening an additional route into storage rather than relying on a single route.
In my liver analogy, there is a normal glucose entry route and an additional insulin-sensitive route.
That extra route, which I associate with GLUT4 in this discussion, opens when insulin rises after eating.
So I describe insulin's role here as opening an extra storage door.
I ask whether that extra door exists in the brain, kidney, or lung, and say no in this framework.
I say the insulin-sensitive route I am discussing is mainly relevant to liver, muscle, and fat tissue.
That is why, in my model, fat storage is especially active around eating.
I contrast this with prolonged fasting, where low insulin is associated with very little fat storage.
I say blood glucose can still be high during fasting because the brain still needs a continuous glucose supply.
The interviewer says the explanation is strong but that the idea now feels much clearer, especially the part about GLUT4.
He notes that insulin is not the only thing that can activate GLUT4.
I agree and say GLUT4 is present mainly in the tissues we have been discussing.
I repeat that these include muscle, fat tissue, and, in my own framework here, the liver.
I say insulin activates it, but other signals do too, including fasting-related states and muscle contraction.
I also mention low cellular ATP or energy demand as another signal associated with increased glucose transport.
I compare this to opening both a door and a window when you want more air in a room.
The point, I say, is to remember that GLUT4 is not present everywhere in the body.
I emphasize that the insulin-sensitive mechanism being discussed is limited to specific tissues.
So, I argue, people should not say that insulin is the hormone responsible for glucose entering every cell in the body.
I finish by saying that statement is false.
